title: Find the pair that adds up
prompt: Given a list of integers and a target, return the indices of two distinct elements whose values add to the target. Explain your approach before writing pseudocode or code.
constraints: A valid pair may not exist; state what your function returns in that case.
Duplicate values and negative numbers are allowed.
You cannot use the same element twice.
hints: Start with a simple solution that checks pairs. What work does it repeat?
As you read a value, ask whether you have already seen its complement.
criteria: I clarified the return value and missing-pair behavior.
I explained a correct approach before coding.
I handled duplicates without reusing one element.
I tested normal, negative, and no-pair cases.
I explained time and space complexity.
outline: Clarify whether any valid pair is acceptable.
Describe checking all pairs, then improve with a map from previously seen values to indices.
Check for target minus current value before storing the current index.
Walk through [3, 3] with target 6 and an input without a pair.
Discuss linear expected time with a hash map and linear additional space.

title: Merge overlapping intervals
prompt: You receive a list of start/end time intervals. Return an ordered list that merges all overlapping intervals. Describe how you know when an interval can be added to the result.
constraints: The input can be empty or unsorted.
Decide whether touching intervals such as [1, 3] and [3, 5] should merge.
State whether your solution changes the input.
hints: What ordering would let you compare only with the most recent merged interval?
Think about the largest endpoint seen in the current group.
criteria: I clarified interval boundaries.
I handled empty and unsorted input.
I explained the sorting step and loop invariant.
I tested nested, disjoint, and touching intervals.
I discussed mutation and complexity.
outline: Clarify endpoint semantics and validate start/end ordering.
Sort by start time, then compare each interval with the final merged interval.
When intervals overlap, extend the end to the maximum endpoint.
Otherwise start a new merged interval.
Explain the sorting cost and the space used for output.

title: Design a URL shortener
prompt: Design a service that turns a long URL into a short link and redirects visitors to the original destination. Walk through requirements, APIs, storage, identifier generation, and operating the service.
constraints: Ask about expected traffic and read/write balance rather than assuming it.
Consider custom aliases, link expiration, and abuse.
Explain the behavior when a destination or short code is missing.
hints: Separate creating a link from serving a redirect.
Compare random codes, counters, and collision handling before picking one.
criteria: I clarified scope and traffic assumptions.
I proposed concrete create and redirect APIs.
I explained code uniqueness and collision handling.
I considered caching, failures, and observability.
I discussed abuse and the trade-offs of my design.
outline: Agree on core features and quantify scale with the interviewer.
Sketch a create endpoint, code-to-destination store, and redirect lookup.
Choose a code generation strategy and explain uniqueness.
Add caching and describe missing, expired, and unsafe-link handling.
Discuss failure modes, metrics, and where you would scale first.

title: Design reliable notifications
prompt: Design a notification service that supports email and in-app messages. Applications submit notification requests, and users control their preferences. Explain how you handle provider failures and duplicate requests.
constraints: The same request may arrive more than once.
Some notifications are time-sensitive; others can wait.
Users can opt out of categories of notifications.
hints: Separate accepting a request from delivering it.
What identifier can make retrying a request safe?
criteria: I clarified channels, priorities, and delivery expectations.
I included user preferences in the flow.
I addressed idempotency and duplicate delivery.
I explained bounded retries and failed-message handling.
I chose useful operational metrics.
outline: Define notification types, urgency, and retention.
Persist requests and process delivery asynchronously.
Use a request identifier and delivery state to reason about duplicates.
Apply preferences, rate limits, retry backoff, and dead-letter handling.
Measure queue age, provider errors, and delivery outcomes.

title: Find the top customers each month
prompt: Given orders(order_id, customer_id, ordered_at, amount, status), find the three highest-spending customers in each calendar month using paid orders only. Explain your query in stages.
constraints: State the timezone used to define a calendar month.
Decide whether ties should produce more than three results.
Explain how you handle null amounts and refunds.
hints: First aggregate paid spend by month and customer.
Then rank customers within each month using the tie behavior you chose.
criteria: I filtered the intended order statuses.
I grouped at the correct month/customer grain.
I chose a ranking function with explicit tie semantics.
I considered nulls, refunds, and timezone.
I checked the output on a small example.
outline: Clarify paid-order and refund semantics.
Build a monthly customer-spend aggregation.
Use a window rank partitioned by month and ordered by spend.
Filter the rank according to the agreed tie policy.
Order the results and discuss relevant indexes after confirming the database.

title: Find users without recent activity
prompt: Given users(user_id, created_at) and events(user_id, occurred_at), find users who have not generated an event in the last 30 days. Explain your approach and test the time boundary.
constraints: Include users who have never generated any event.
Decide whether an event exactly on the boundary counts as recent.
Multiple events per user must not duplicate output users.
hints: Think in terms of the absence of a matching recent event.
Compare NOT EXISTS with a carefully constrained outer join.
criteria: I included never-active users.
I defined the 30-day boundary.
I avoided duplicate output users.
I explained the absence check.
I considered an index on event user and time.
outline: Define now and the time boundary consistently.
Use NOT EXISTS for a matching recent event per user, or an equivalent outer join.
Keep the recent-event condition in the correct part of the query.
Test never-active, old-only, and boundary-event users.
Discuss how an event index supports the lookup.

title: Tell a story about difficult feedback
prompt: Tell me about a time you received feedback that was difficult to hear. What did you do with it, and what changed? Use a real example and keep confidential details out of your notes.
constraints: Explain your own actions, not only what the team did.
Acknowledge what you initially found difficult.
Use evidence of change rather than an invented metric.
hints: Keep the situation brief so your actions have room.
What would the person who gave the feedback say changed afterward?
criteria: I chose a specific, honest example.
I described the feedback without defensiveness.
I explained an action I took.
I gave credible evidence of what changed.
I reflected on what I would do next time.
outline: Set the context and describe the feedback.
Explain your initial reaction and how you clarified it.
Describe the change you tried and how you followed up.
Share a concrete outcome or observation.
Close with what you learned and how you now approach feedback.

title: Respond to a failing deployment
prompt: A new deployment has increased request failures. Walk through your first response, the evidence you would collect, how you would decide whether to roll back, and the follow-up work.
constraints: Customer impact is ongoing; explain how you prioritize mitigation.
You do not yet know whether the application or infrastructure is at fault.
A rollback may be complicated by database changes.
hints: Separate restoring service from finding the root cause.
What did the deployment change, and what evidence can compare old and new behavior?
criteria: I established impact and communicated clearly.
I chose useful metrics, logs, and deployment comparisons.
I prioritized safe mitigation.
I considered rollback and data compatibility.
I described a learning-focused follow-up.
outline: Establish severity, recent changes, and incident ownership.
Check errors, latency, saturation, logs, and rollout state.
Choose a safe rollback, traffic shift, or other mitigation based on evidence.
Consider schema compatibility and verify service recovery.
Capture a timeline and prevention actions after the incident.
